myriad

MEER-ee-ud -- stress on the first syllable, MEER. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Myriad is countless or great in number.

From the ship's dark deck, the passengers gazed up at a myriad of stars strewn across the moonless sky.

Example

The tide pools hold so many barnacles that the biologist gives up counting at four hundred and simply writes 'beyond counting' in her field notebook.

The barnacles exist in a myriad -- a number so great that counting them is hopeless. A myriad is a countless multitude, an amount that overwhelms any attempt to number it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

host: A host is a large number of people or things -- a host of volunteers, a host of reasons -- big, but still the kind of number you could tally. A myriad goes far beyond that: a quantity so vast that counting becomes hopeless. A host is many; a myriad is past numbering.

torrent: A torrent is a violent, rushing stream of something -- floodwater, angry emails, rapid-fire questions -- arriving fast and hard. A myriad is about count, not motion: an uncountably vast number that may sit perfectly still. A torrent rushes at you; a myriad simply outnumbers you.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

handful: a small number

smattering: a small sprinkling of something

Where it sits · how far past counting it goes — multitude → myriad → profusion

multitude vs. myriad: Multitude is large but still countable, so it is weaker than myriad -- a multitude fills a stadium, while a myriad defeats counting altogether: stars, sand grains, snowflakes.

profusion vs. myriad: Profusion presses even harder than myriad: a myriad is a count too high to finish, while a profusion overflows -- an extravagant outpouring that spills past every container.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — myri-

root — myri-: ten thousand; countless (Greek myrias)

suffix — -ad

suffix — -ad: Greek number-group ending (as in triad, decade) (Greek)

Put it together

Put it together: Greek myrias meant 'ten thousand' -- the largest number Greek named with a single word -- and -ad is the Greek ending for number groups, as in triad and decade. Because ten thousand sat at the edge of easy counting, myriad slid from 'ten thousand exactly' to 'countless.'

Use the root in a new word: myriapod

Use the root in a new word: myriapod: The centipede in the woodpile is a myriapod, though it has far fewer than a hundred legs.

Root Check

Word Choice

Myriad works two ways: as a noun with 'of' ('a myriad of choices') and directly before a plural ('myriad choices'); both are correct, whatever grammar folklore claims. It stresses sheer uncountable quantity -- stars, options, details -- and it needs no help from 'countless' or 'endless,' which would double the meaning.
